extra.message: The raw HTTP request body (or the `blob` query parameter, optionally base64-decoded) is passed directly to `pickle.loads()`. Unpickling attacker-controlled data results in arbitrary code execution via crafted `__reduce__` payloads.

The `expr` query parameter is passed to `eval()`. The empty `__builtins__` sandbox is not a security boundary — Python object-graph traversal (e.g. via `().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()`) allows recovery of builtins and arbitrary code execution.

The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated into a Jinja2 `Template` source string and rendered. Attacker-controlled template syntax is evaluated server-side (SSTI), which in Jinja2 leads to sandbox escape and remote code execution, as well as reflected XSS since the result is returned as text/html.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code (Code Injection)

extra.message: The `name` query parameter is joined onto `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` with no canonicalisation or confinement check, and the request body is written to the resulting path. A value such as `../../payroll/views.py` or `../../../../etc/cron.d/x` escapes the export directory, allowing arbitrary file write and thus remote code execution.

cwe: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path

extra.message: The `ref` query parameter is interpolated into the export file path (`BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json"`) without normalisation, so `ref=../../config/settings` writes outside the intended directory and overwrites arbitrary files. The written JSON also persists SSN and card number values in cleartext on disk.

cwe: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path

extra.message: The lxml parser is explicitly configured with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True` and `no_network=False`, then used to parse the attacker-supplied request body. This permits XML External Entity attacks: local file disclosure (`file:///etc/passwd`), SSRF, and billion-laughs style denial of service.

cwe: CWE-611: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

extra.message: The JSON request body is used directly as the MongoDB query document passed to `find_one()`. An attacker can inject query operators (e.g. `{"filter": {"$ne": null}}` or `{"$where": "..."}`) to bypass intended filtering and read arbitrary documents from the `ops.records` collection.

cwe: CWE-943: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic

extra.message: The `endpoint` query parameter is fetched with `urllib.request.urlopen()` with no scheme allowlist or host validation, and the response body is echoed back to the caller. This is a full read-capable SSRF: internal services and cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254) can be reached, and `file://` URLs allow local file disclosure.

The privilege decision is made entirely from a client-supplied value: the `ops_badge` cookie or `x-ops-badge` header. Any caller who sets `ops_badge=lead` receives the elevated response (`payroll: full`). Authorization must be derived from authoritative server-side identity/session state, never from request-controlled input.

cwe: CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision

extra.message: The financial `amount` and the approval `state` of the ledger are taken directly from the request body / query string with no server-side validation or authorization check. A caller can set `state=approved` and an arbitrary (including negative) `amount` to manipulate the balance and approval decision. `int()` on unvalidated input also raises an unhandled ValueError.

cwe: CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision

extra.message: The `hr_approve` and `make_effective` transitions check only the actor's role, never that the actor is not the subject or the requester. The manager branch on line 241 explicitly enforces `comp.employee.user_id != request.user.id`, but the HR branches do not. An HR admin can therefore create a compensation request for their own profile (line 210 returns all employees for HR_ADMIN, and line 217 pre-sets it to `manager_approved`), then approve it and make it effective, self-granting a salary increase. `CompensationRequest.clean()` (models.py:85) contains the separation-of-duty rule but is never invoked on these transitions because the view mutates `status` and calls `save()` without `full_clean()`.

Every user account created through the CSV employee import is assigned the hardcoded password `ChangeMe123!`, with no forced reset, no expiry and no notification. Anyone who knows this constant (it is in the source tree) can authenticate as any imported employee, and the accounts are usable indefinitely. Contrast employee_invite (line 138) which generates a random password.

The verification secrets for the `north` and `south` handles are hardcoded in source as a dict of 4-digit values, and are compared with a non-constant-time `!=`. Anyone with source access authenticates trivially, and the 4-digit keyspace is exhaustible in ~10000 requests since the endpoint applies no rate limiting or lockout (see the separate CWE-307 finding).

`SECRET_KEY` silently falls back to the hardcoded literal `dev-only-change-me` when `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` is unset. If deployed without that environment variable, an attacker who knows this public constant can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens and signed cookies, achieving full authentication bypass. The application should refuse to start instead of defaulting.

`DEBUG` defaults to True (`os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "1") == "1"`) — debug mode is active unless explicitly disabled. In production this exposes full tracebacks with source snippets, local variable values, settings (including database credentials) and SQL queries on any unhandled exception. It additionally enables the unauthenticated MEDIA_ROOT file server at config/urls.py:26-27, exposing every uploaded HR document, payslip and onboarding evidence file without any authorization check. The default must be fail-secure (False).

When DEBUG is on (the default, settings.py:9) all of MEDIA_ROOT is served at /media/ with no authentication or authorization. The `document_download` view carefully enforces `can_view_document`, but the underlying files in `hr_documents/` and `onboarding_evidence/` are reachable directly by URL, bypassing every role and ownership check on payslips, tax forms and contracts.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: The `lane` query parameter is passed straight to `redirect()` with no allowlist or same-origin check, so `?lane=https://evil.example/login` sends the victim to an attacker-controlled site under the application's trust context — usable for credential phishing and token leakage.

cwe: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site (Open Redirect)

extra.message: The full raw request body (compensation intake data — salaries, PII) and the `Authorization` header (bearer token / credentials) are written verbatim to the application log at WARNING level. Log files, aggregators and error trackers are far more widely readable than the payroll database, so this leaks credentials and sensitive personal data to anyone with log access.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

extra.message: The exception handler returns the raw exception string and the exception class name to the client. The message embeds the server-side absolute filesystem path (`BASE_EXPORT_DIR`) plus the reflected `lot_ref` input, disclosing internal deployment layout that aids path-traversal and further attacks.

cwe: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

extra.message: The request's `Origin` header is reflected verbatim into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` while `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is set to `true`. This makes every origin a trusted origin: any malicious site can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint using the victim's session cookie and read the responses, defeating the same-origin policy.

The response explicitly disables browser protections: `X-XSS-Protection: 0` turns off the legacy XSS auditor and `Content-Security-Policy: ""` emits an empty policy. This removes defence-in-depth against script injection and framing for this endpoint's responses.

`set_cookie("portal_crumb", marker)` is called without `httponly=True`, `secure=True` or a `samesite` value, and the cookie value is fully attacker-controlled via the `marker` query parameter. The cookie is readable by any JavaScript on the page and transmitted over plaintext HTTP, and the unsanitised value permits cookie/header manipulation.

A nonce/verification code is generated with `random.choice()`, which is backed by the deterministic, non-cryptographic Mersenne Twister. Observing a modest number of generated codes lets an attacker recover the PRNG state and predict all future codes. `secrets.choice` / `get_random_string` must be used for security tokens. The caller-controlled `length` is also unvalidated (`length=0` yields an empty code; a huge value is a DoS lever).

cwe: CWE-338: Use of Cryptographically Weak PRNG

extra.message: `ssl._create_unverified_context()` is used for the outbound HTTPS call to the partner endpoint, disabling both certificate-chain and hostname verification. Any network-position attacker can transparently man-in-the-middle this payroll partner connection to read or alter the data in transit.

The login endpoint uses Django's stock `LoginView` with no rate limiting, throttling, account lockout, CAPTCHA or failed-attempt counter anywhere in the request path — MIDDLEWARE (settings.py:22-31) contains no throttling component and no such control exists in the app. Credentials can be brute-forced or password-sprayed without limit, and the same applies to the `password_reset` endpoint (line 12) which additionally permits unbounded outbound email generation.

cwe: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

extra.message: This verifier-check endpoint applies no rate limiting, attempt counting or lockout, and the verifier values are only 4 digits (line 116). The complete keyspace can be exhausted in ~10,000 unthrottled requests. The endpoint also acts as a handle oracle, returning 404 for unknown handles versus 403 for a bad verifier (user enumeration).

cwe: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

extra.message: `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE` and `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE` are never set (default False), and `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`, `SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS` and `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` are absent, even though `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` shows the app runs behind a TLS-terminating proxy. Session and CSRF cookies for this HR/payroll application are therefore transmitted over plaintext HTTP and can be captured by a network attacker, enabling session hijacking.

Authorization failures produce no durable security audit event: `require_role` and every `can_view_*` rejection simply raises `PermissionDenied`, and the `audit()` helper (views.py:51) is only ever invoked on successful paths. There is no LOGGING configuration in settings.py, no signal receiver for `user_login_failed`, and no middleware that records denials — so failed logins, blocked attempts to read other employees' compensation (views.py:163-164, 229-230), and rejected document downloads (views.py:345-346) leave no trace. Enumeration and privilege-escalation probing against this payroll system is therefore undetectable.

`policy_list` returns every active Policy to any authenticated user, ignoring the `audience` field (models.py:152 defines `managers`, `payroll` and `hr` audiences). An employee-role user can read HR-internal and payroll-internal policy bodies, and `policy_ack` (line 429-431) likewise lets them acknowledge policies not addressed to them. The dashboard employee branch (line 100) has the same defect.
